The chemical element phosphorus 
Phosphorus was first discovered in 1669 by German physician Hennig Brand. Brand is a well-
known name in chemistry as he is sometimes called the last of the alchemists. Alchemists 
sought a method of changing lead, iron, and other metals into gold, as well as the secret of 
eternal life. Alchemy was practised from around 500 BC to the late 1600s, but it contained too 
much magic and mysticism to be considered a real science. However, it did develop a number 
of scientific techniques and produced many new materials that were later found to have 
valuable applications in modern chemistry. 
 
Brand was convinced that the key to changing metals into gold could be discovered in urine. 
His experiments to find such a chemical were, of course, a failure, but he made an accidental 
discovery along the way: in the process of heating and purifying urine, he obtained a material 
which mysteriously glowed green in the dark - phosphorus. In doing so, he became the first 
known discoverer of an element. Other elements such as gold and silver had been known 
since ancient times, but there is no record of who discovered them. Brand named the new 
substance phosphorus after the Greek for 'light bearer'. At a time when light was usually 
produced by burning materials, his discovery was a source of great curiosity. Although, like 
many alchemists, he was secretive about his methods, they eventually became widely known. 
 
Other scientists began to experiment with the element, and phosphorus soon became a 
wonder of 17th-century European courts and fairs, with the chemiluminescent combination 
of phosphorus and atmospheric oxygen producing a light show no one had ever seen before 
or even thought possible. It was hoped that phosphorus might offer a safer alternative to 
candles for lighting the home, until people realised that it could catch fire spontaneously. The 
17th-century chemist Nicolas Lemery discovered this for himself when, in his hurry to go out 
following an experiment, he left a small piece of phosphorus on a table in his house. A maid 
later placed some clean bed sheets on top of it, in preparation for changing the bed covers. 
The phosphorus got caught up in the sheets and the next occupant of the bed was lucky to 
escape with his life when the bed later caught fire. 
 
Despite such accidents, the new element seemed to offer a path to wealth and fame, although 
Brand himself showed little interest in its potential. Not much is known about what happened 
to him after his discovery, and there is no record of where or when he died. Ten years after 
Brand's discovery, the Anglo-Irish philosopher, scientist, and inventor Robert Boyle added 
silicon dioxide to phosphorus, then coated paper with the resulting mixture. When he drew a

wood splinter through the paper, it caught fire, producing the first match. He later discovered 
that using white phosphorus for match heads meant that a flame could be produced with only 
the slightest heat from friction. It was seen as a huge step forward at a time when lighting a 
fire was a very labour-intensive task. 
 
White phosphorus (also referred to as yellow phosphorus) had been discovered by Brand, but 
there are other forms; red phosphorus and, the most stable form, black, or violet phosphorus. 
The three forms all have different physical and chemical properties. White phosphorus is a 
transparent solid, similar in appearance to wax. It is extremely flammable, spontaneously 
catching fire in temperatures above 30°C. For this reason, it has to be kept in water when not 
in use. Although originally used in the production of matches, it is poisonous and can cause 
liver damage. The first cases of phosphorus poisoning presented themselves in the 1850s, but 
white phosphorus continued to be used until the early 20th century, when it was finally 
replaced with the much safer red phosphorus that still adorns the side of match-boxes. 
 
Red phosphorus is a red powder which can be made by heating white phosphorus. Although 
flammable, it will only ignite at temperatures above 240°C and this level of stability makes it 
safer to work with than white phosphorus. Interestingly, it can also be used to make products 
called fire retardants, which slow or stop the spread of fire. 
 
In terms of appearance, properties and structure, black phosphorus, also referred to as violet 
phosphorus, has much in common with graphite. Black phosphorus can be synthesized from 
red phosphorus, under extreme pressure and high temperatures. One of the significant 
properties of black phosphorus is that, despite not being a metal, it can conduct electricity. In 
recent years, engineers have become interested in its potential use in the manufacture of 
electronics. It is hoped that devices could be made smaller if black phosphorus is used in their 
production instead of silicon.
